# (PART) The rules {-}

# Rage Generation {#rage}

```{r setup-rage, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
theme_set(theme_minimal())
# Every plot in the book starts its value axis at 0, so differences aren't exaggerated. This wraps
# ggplot() for all chapters; plots whose values are on the x axis set that separately.
ggplot <- function(...) ggplot2::ggplot(...) + ggplot2::expand_limits(y = 0)
set.seed(1234)
clusters <- read_csv("data/derived/swing_clusters.csv")
swings   <- read_csv("data/derived/swings.csv")
energize <- read_csv("data/derived/energize.csv")
procs    <- read_csv("data/derived/procs.csv")
ubw_hand <- read_csv("data/derived/ubw_by_hand.csv")
ubw5     <- filter(procs, ubw_rank == 5)
ubw_rate <- sum(ubw5$ubw_procs) / sum(ubw5$landed_white)   # Unbridled Wrath proc rate at 5/5
meta     <- yaml::read_yaml("data/logs/metadata.yaml")

conv <- function(lvl) 0.0091107836 * lvl^2 + 3.225598133 * lvl + 4.2652911
# Classic (1.12) rage per point of damage, divided by C. Kalgan's blue post (2006), ClassicSim and WarriorSim
# all use 7.5. The Classic compendium used 15, which gave Classic twice its real rage.
classic_k <- 7.5
source("data/fight_sim.R")  # the talent profiles (`forever_talents`) and the fight simulator, shared with the later chapters

# Speed and hand for each swing: the posted weapon speed nearest to the measured swing interval,
# and main vs off hand from the rate (off-hand rates are about half the main-hand ones).
weapons <- map_dfr(meta, ~ tibble(file = .x$file, speed = map_dbl(.x$equipped_weapons, "speed"),
                                  weapon = map_chr(.x$equipped_weapons, "name")))
cl <- clusters %>%
  mutate(speed = map2_dbl(file, swing_interval_median,
                          ~ { s <- weapons$speed[weapons$file == .x]; s[which.min(abs(s - .y))] }),
         rate  = mean_gain / speed,
         hand  = case_when(setup == "two_hand" ~ "Two-hand", rate > 2.5 ~ "Main hand", TRUE ~ "Off hand"))

obs <- swings %>% filter(!capped) %>%
  mutate(gain = gain / 10) %>%
  left_join(cl %>% select(file, lo = mean_gain, speed, hand), by = "file", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  filter(abs(gain - lo) <= 0.2) %>%
  left_join(weapons, by = c("file", "speed")) %>%
  mutate(classic = classic_k * damage / conv(level),
         group   = paste0(character, ", ", hand, " ", speed))

fmt_p <- function(p) format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 1e-10)

# The measured Forever rates, used by the later chapters: rage per second of weapon speed for each hand.
forever_mh <- with(filter(obs, hand == "Main hand"), mean(gain / speed))
forever_oh <- with(filter(obs, hand == "Off hand"),  mean(gain / speed))
forever_dw <- forever_mh + forever_oh          # no talents
# Rage per second of weapon speed for every logged swing, which the simulations draw from
forever_draws <- list(MH = with(filter(obs, hand == "Main hand"), gain / speed),
                      OH = with(filter(obs, hand == "Off hand"),  gain / speed))

# Chapter version: newest first. See "Changelog" at the end of the chapter for what each part means.
changelog <- tribble(
  ~version, ~date,        ~change,

*Version `r changelog$version[1]` (`r changelog$date[1]`), based on `r length(meta)` logs from beta build 1.60.1. See the [changelog](#rage-changelog) for what changed.*

## The formula {#rage-formula}

A white hit is a normal auto attack (so not an ability like Heroic Strike). In Forever, the rage from a white hit depends on just two things: the hand that made the swing, and the weapon's speed. Since 1 October, crits and Dual Wield Specialization also multiply it.

\begin{equation}
Rage = r_{hand} \times speed \times m_{crit} \times m_{DWS}
\end{equation}

Where:

- $speed$ is the weapon speed on the tooltip (for example, 2.6 for Vileblood Scimitar). It's not the time the swing actually took, so haste doesn't shrink it (see [Haste](#haste)).
- $r_{hand}$ is the rate, which is the rage for each second of weapon speed. It's about **3.5** in the main hand (we measured `r round(forever_mh, 2)`), **half that, 1.75**, in the off hand (`r round(forever_oh, 2)`), and **4.5** with a two-hander.
- $m_{crit}$ is `r forever_talents$crit_rage_mult` on a critical strike and 1 otherwise.
- $m_{DWS}$ is Dual Wield Specialization's bonus to off-hand rage: `r forever_talents$oh_rage_mult` at 5/5 (10% a point). It's 1 for the main hand, for a two-hander and without the talent.

Example: a 2.6 speed main hand gives $`r round(forever_mh, 2)` \times 2.6 = `r sprintf("%.1f", forever_mh * 2.6)`$ rage per hit and `r sprintf("%.1f", forever_mh * 2.6 * forever_talents$crit_rage_mult)` on a crit, whether the hit does 100 damage or 1000.

Some of this formula is measured in our logs, and some only comes from Blizzard so far:

```{r}
tribble(
  ~Part,                                                        ~`Where it comes from`,
  "The rate for each hand, times weapon speed",                  "Measured in our logs (below)",
  "Damage, attack power and level don't change it",              "Measured in our logs (below)",
  "A hasted swing still gives the full rage",                    "Measured in our logs (Haste section)",
  "A crit gives twice the rage",                                 "Blizzard's 1 Oct notes, edited 2 Oct. Our logs are older and show no crit bonus. Not yet checked in a log",
  "Dual Wield Specialization: +50% off-hand rage at 5/5",        "The hotfixed talent tooltip (Blizzard's notes say it gives none). Not yet checked in a log"
) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Where each part of the formula comes from.")
```

Blizzard's [30 September announcement](https://worldofwarcraft.blizzard.com/en-us/news/24301514) also said that rage from dealing damage is now "normalised" to weapon speed, which is what our logs found. [How the Rules Changed](#rules-history) lists every change to rage since our logs were recorded.

### How this differs from Classic

In Classic, rage came from damage. Each white hit gave:

\begin{equation}
Rage = \frac{D}{C} \times 7.5
\end{equation}

$D$ is the damage of the hit, and $C$ is the rage conversion value, which grows with your level ($C = 0.0091107836 \times Lvl^2 + 3.225598133 \times Lvl + 4.2652911$, about `r round(conv(60))` at level 60). Blizzard gave the 7.5 in a [blue post by Kalgan](https://www.bluetracker.gg/wow/topic/eu-en/83678537-the-new-rage-formula-by-kalgan/), and both Classic simulators, [WarriorSim](https://github.com/GuybrushGit/WarriorSim) and [ClassicSim](https://github.com/timhul/ClassicSim), use it. The [Classic compendium](https://01a0bad7-106c-87b4-a48f-17061469cc4d.share.connect.posit.cloud/) used 15, which gave Classic twice its real rage, and earlier versions of this book copied that.

So in Classic, anything that made you hit harder gave you more rage: a better weapon, more attack power, and crits, which double the damage. The same hit was also worth less rage at a higher level. In Forever, only weapon speed matters, plus the crit and Dual Wield Specialization multipliers. Gear can raise your rage only through crit and haste. The [How Damage Scales chapter](#scaling) works out what that means as your gear improves.

## The logs

So far we've looked at `r length(meta)` combat logs, some posted to the [forever-warrior discussions](https://github.com/magey/forever-warrior/discussions) and some shared with us directly, all on beta build 1.60.1. The nice thing about these logs is that they record the warrior's current rage on almost every event, so we can read the rage from a single white swing straight off the log instead of having to guess at it.

```{r}
tibble(
  Log       = map_chr(meta, "character_name"),
  Setup     = map_chr(meta, "setup"),
  Weapons   = map_chr(meta, ~ paste0(map_chr(.x$equipped_weapons, "name"), " (",
                                   map_dbl(.x$equipped_weapons, "speed"), ")", collapse = " / ")),
  Source    = map_chr(meta, "source")
) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Logs and the metadata posted with them (main hand first).")
```

We left out any swing made while sitting at 100 rage, since the cap cuts off whatever that swing would have given.

## What the logs show

```{r}
clusters %>%
  transmute(Character = character, Setup = setup,
            `Swing interval (s)` = round(swing_interval_median, 2),
            `Rage per swing` = round(mean_gain, 2),
            `Rage per second of swing interval` = round(mean_gain / swing_interval_median, 2),
            `Damage range` = paste(damage_min, damage_max, sep = "-"),
            `Crit` = round(mean_gain_crit, 2), `Non-crit` = round(mean_gain_noncrit, 2),
            Swings = n) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rage per white swing, grouped by the distinct values observed. Rage per second of swing interval uses the measured interval, so it reads high for Ceece's two-hander, where half the swings were hasted by Fishliver Oil (see the Haste section).")
```

```{r fig.cap="Rage per swing against damage dealt. Each group is flat: damage does not change the rage gained."}
swings %>% filter(!capped) %>%
  ggplot(aes(damage, gain / 10, colour = character)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.05, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ setup) +
  labs(x = "Damage dealt", y = "Rage gained", colour = NULL)
```

```{r}
lv_seen <- range(obs$level[obs$level > 0])
```

1. **Damage doesn't change rage.** Within each group, the damage varies by 2 to 4 times, but the rage stays the same. Under Classic's formula, the rage would follow the damage.
2. **Rage is a fixed rate times weapon speed.** The time between swings in each group lines up with one of the posted weapon speeds, and the rage per swing is that speed times a fixed rate for each hand (the table and figure below). The off-hand rate is exactly half the main-hand rate. Two-handers at `r paste(sort(unique(obs$speed[obs$hand == "Two-hand"])), collapse = ", ")` speed all land on the same line. If two-handers got the one-hand rate plus a fixed bonus for each swing, the slower ones would sit below that line.
3. **Weapon speed doesn't change your rage per second.** A slow weapon gives more rage per swing but swings less often, so fast and slow weapons give rage at the same rate over time.
4. **Level doesn't change it.** Characters from level `r lv_seen[1]` to `r lv_seen[2]` all get the same rates, and so does a level 1 character in the haste test. Over that range, the Classic formula would give `r round((1 - conv(lv_seen[1]) / conv(lv_seen[2])) * 100)`% less rage for the same hit. None of our logs is above level `r lv_seen[2]`, so higher levels still need checking.
5. **In these logs, crits and glancing blows gave the same rage as a normal hit.** That was the rule in build 1.60.1, which all our logs come from. Since 1 October, a crit gives twice the rage (see [the formula](#rage-formula)). No log has checked that yet, or whether glancing blows still give the full rage.

```{r}
obs %>% mutate(rate = gain / speed) %>% group_by(Hand = hand) %>%
  summarise(m = mean(rate), se = sd(rate) / sqrt(n()), Swings = n(),
            Speeds = paste(sort(unique(speed)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  transmute(Hand, `Rage per second of weapon speed` = round(m, 2),
            `95% interval` = sprintf("%.3f to %.3f", m - 1.96 * se, m + 1.96 * se),
            `Weapon speeds logged` = Speeds, Swings) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "The rate for each hand, from every logged swing below the rage cap. The 95% intervals are very narrow, because each weapon gives almost exactly the same rage on every swing.")
```

```{r fig.cap="Rage per swing against weapon speed, for every logged swing (dots). The dashed lines are the rate times weapon speed for each hand, starting at zero. Every weapon lands on its hand's line."}
rate_lines <- obs %>% group_by(hand) %>% summarise(rate = mean(gain / speed), .groups = "drop")
ggplot(obs, aes(speed, gain, colour = hand)) +
  geom_abline(data = rate_lines, aes(slope = rate, intercept = 0, colour = hand), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.03, height = 0, alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  expand_limits(x = 0) +
  labs(x = "Weapon speed", y = "Rage per swing", colour = NULL)
```

## Haste {#haste}

In Forever, each swing gives rate x weapon speed rage. That leaves one important question: when something makes you swing faster, does each swing still give the full amount, or does the game shrink it to match the shorter swing? If it's the full amount, haste gives you more rage per second, just like it gives you more damage. If it shrinks, haste does nothing for rage.

Two posters tested this. elvenfresh recorded a level 1 Troll using **Berserking** (their racial, which gives 10% attack speed at full health), and Ceece recorded two fights with **Fishliver Oil**, which in Forever turns out to give about 10% attack speed for 30 seconds. For every swing, we know whether the buff was up, how long since the last swing, and how much rage it gave:

```{r}
haste <- read_csv("data/derived/haste.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(label = paste0(character, ": ", buff, " (", speed, " speed)"))
haste_tbl <- haste %>% group_by(label, speed, hasted) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), interval = median(interval, na.rm = TRUE), gain = mean(gain), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = hasted, values_from = c(n, interval, gain)) %>%
  mutate(speedup = interval_FALSE / interval_TRUE - 1,
         model = if_else(grepl("Rock Hammer|3.7", label), 4.5, 3.46) * speed)
haste_tbl %>%
  transmute(Log = label,
            `Swing time (normal / hasted)` = sprintf("%.2f / %.2f sec", interval_FALSE, interval_TRUE),
            `Faster by` = sprintf("%.0f%%", speedup * 100),
            `Rage per swing, normal` = sprintf("%.2f (n = %d)", gain_FALSE, n_FALSE),
            `Rage per swing, hasted` = sprintf("%.2f (n = %d)", gain_TRUE, n_TRUE),
            `If rage shrank with the swing` = sprintf("%.2f", gain_FALSE / (1 + speedup))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rage per landed white swing with and without a haste buff. The last column is what a hasted swing would give if the game scaled rage to the shorter swing time.")
```

```{r fig.cap="Every landed white swing in the three haste logs: the rage it gave (left) and the time since the previous swing (right), without and with the haste buff. The buff makes swings come about 10% sooner, but each one still gives the same rage.", fig.height=4.2}
haste %>%
  select(label, hasted, `Time since the last swing (sec)` = interval, `Rage from the swing` = gain) %>%
  pivot_longer(-c(label, hasted)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(value), !(name == "Time since the last swing (sec)" & value > 5)) %>%
  mutate(hasted = if_else(hasted, "Hasted", "Normal")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(label, value, colour = hasted)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitterdodge(jitter.width = 0.15, dodge.width = 0.6), alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ name, scales = "free_x") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Normal = "grey55", Hasted = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
n_hasted <- sum(haste$hasted)
haste_diff <- haste %>% group_by(label) %>% summarise(d = mean(gain[hasted]) - mean(gain[!hasted])) %>% pull(d)
```

**Haste doesn't shrink the rage from a swing.** All `r n_hasted` hasted swings gave the normal rate x weapon speed, within the 0.1 rage the log rounds to (the averages differ by at most `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(haste_diff)))` rage), and none came anywhere near the smaller amount they would give if the game scaled rage to the shorter swing time. Since rage per swing is always exactly the same in Forever, this doesn't need a p-value: a single hasted swing at full rage is enough to rule out the shrinking version, and we have `r n_hasted`.

So **in Forever, haste is a rage stat**: 10% faster swings give 10% more white rage per second. That matters for Flurry (see the [Flurry chapter](#flurry)), Berserking, haste potions and any haste on gear, and it's one of the few ways left to raise your rage with gear. Every bit of haste counts, too: there's no "breakpoint" you need to reach before it pays off (see [Haste breakpoints](#haste-breakpoints)).

## Other rage sources

```{r}
energize %>% filter(amount > 0) %>% mutate(Log = str_remove(file, "_092326.txt")) %>% group_by(Log, spell) %>%
  summarise(`Typical amount` = amount[which.max(n)], Events = sum(n)) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Rage granted directly by abilities and talents (amounts below the typical value were cut off by the cap).")
```

- **Charge** gives 9 rage and **Bloodrage** gives 10 up front plus 1 per tick, same as in Classic.
- **Unbridled Wrath** gives 1 rage per proc with one-handers but 2 with the two-hander, which fits the same pattern of two-handers getting more rage per event. (Blizzard's 1 Oct notes take that away: two-handers get 1 rage per proc now too.)
- **Unbridled Wrath procs a lot less often than its tooltip says** (a bug), and never off Heroic Strike or Cleave. There's a whole section on it below.
- **Heroic Strike** hits don't give any rage, at least in the cases we checked.
- **Misses, dodges and parries** on our own swings give little or no rage (though we only have a few of them).
- **Rage from damage taken** is small, but it varied between logs, so it needs a proper controlled test.
- **Reckless Swings**, a Fury talent added on 2 November (row 4, so not in any of our logs), is a new direct source: for 25% of your base health, your next 4 melee attacks within 8 seconds give 5 extra rage each, on a 15-second cooldown. That's up to 20 rage every 15 seconds, or 1.33 rage per second, a little more than Dual Wield Specialization's whole off-hand rage bonus. The [Reckless Swings section](#reckless-swings) of the How Damage Scales chapter works out what it's worth.

### Unbridled Wrath

Unbridled Wrath is meant to give a 12% chance per talent point to gain rage on a white hit, so 60% at 5/5. To test that, Tarch recorded the same fights with 1, 2, 3 and 4 points in the talent (and nothing else but 5/5 Cruelty), and Zomd's logs were recorded at 5/5. That gives us the proc rate at every talent rank:

```{r}
ubw <- procs %>% filter(!is.na(ubw_rank)) %>%
  group_by(rank = ubw_rank) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(landed_white), k = sum(ubw_procs), .groups = "drop")

# Best estimate of the chance per talent point, assuming each point adds the same chance
# (maximum likelihood over all ranks together).
per_point <- optimize(function(q) -sum(dbinom(ubw$k, ubw$n, pmin(q * ubw$rank, 1), log = TRUE)),
                      c(0.01, 0.2))$minimum

ubw %>%
  transmute(`Talent points` = paste0(rank, "/5"), `Landed white hits` = n, Procs = k,
            `Proc rate` = sprintf("%.1f%%", k / n * 100),
            `95% interval` = sprintf("%.1f%% to %.1f%%", qbeta(0.025, k + 1, n - k + 1) * 100,
                                     qbeta(0.975, k + 1, n - k + 1) * 100),
            `Expected at 12% per point` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 12 * rank),
            `p-value vs 12% per point` = map2_chr(k, n, ~ fmt_p(binom.test(.x, .y, 0.12 * ubw$rank[ubw$k == .x & ubw$n == .y])$p.value)),
            `Expected at 8% per point` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 8 * rank),
            `p-value vs 8% per point` = map2_chr(k, n, ~ fmt_p(binom.test(.x, .y, 0.08 * ubw$rank[ubw$k == .x & ubw$n == .y])$p.value))) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "How often Unbridled Wrath procs on a landed white hit, by talent points. The 95% interval comes from a Bayesian posterior with a flat prior. A small p-value means the logs are very unlikely at that proc rate.")
```

```{r fig.cap="Unbridled Wrath's proc rate at each talent rank (dots, with 95% intervals), against 12% per point (what the talent should give, dashed) and 8% per point (dotted). The logs follow the lower line.", fig.height=3.5}
ubw %>% mutate(rate = k / n, lo = qbeta(0.025, k + 1, n - k + 1), hi = qbeta(0.975, k + 1, n - k + 1)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(rank, rate)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 0.12, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_abline(slope = 0.08, intercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.6, y = 0.12 * 4.6, label = "12% per point", hjust = 1, vjust = -0.6, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.6, y = 0.08 * 4.6, label = "8% per point", hjust = 0, vjust = 1.6, size = 3, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:5, labels = paste0(1:5, "/5"), limits = c(0.8, 5.2)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.65)) +
  labs(x = "Points in Unbridled Wrath", y = "Procs per landed white hit")
```

The talent clearly doesn't give 12% per point: that's rejected at every rank (only just at 1/5, where we have the fewest procs). Our best estimate is about **`r round(per_point * 100, 1)`% per point**, and 5/5 lands at `r round(ubw$k[ubw$rank == 5] / ubw$n[ubw$rank == 5] * 100)`%, a long way from 60%. The tooltip says 12% per point, so this is a bug: it's close to the 8% per point Classic's Unbridled Wrath had (40% at 5/5), so the beta may still be using the old Classic chance. It's listed as [BUG-1](#bug-ubw) in the Known Bugs chapter. The developers have confirmed it and a fix is coming in a future beta build ([issue #105](https://github.com/ClassicWoWCommunity/forever-bugs/issues/105)). Siax's rank wasn't posted, but his proc rate (`r round(procs$ubw_procs[procs$character == "Siax"] / procs$landed_white[procs$character == "Siax"] * 100)`%) matches 5/5.

#### Does weapon speed matter? {#ubw-ppm}

Some procs in the game work on "procs per minute" (PPM): instead of a fixed chance on every hit, the chance scales with weapon speed, so a slow weapon gets a bigger chance on each swing and every weapon ends up with about the same number of procs per minute. This was asked in the [forever-warrior issues](https://github.com/magey/forever-warrior/issues/4), since the low proc rate could have been PPM working out lower than 60% for common weapon speeds.

We can test that by splitting the procs by which weapon made the hit. Each proc shows up in the log a few milliseconds after the white hit that caused it, and each weapon gives its own, known amount of rage per hit (rate × speed, from earlier in this chapter), so we can tell main hand, off hand and two-hander hits apart. If it were PPM, the proc chance per hit would grow in line with the weapon speed, so a 3.8 two-hander would proc about twice as often per hit as a 1.8 off hand.

```{r}
ubw_hand_rk <- ubw_hand %>% filter(!is.na(ubw_rank))
ubw_hand_rk %>%
  group_by(Character = character, `Talent points` = paste0(ubw_rank, "/5"),
           Weapon = recode(hand, main_hand = "Main hand", off_hand = "Off hand", two_hand = "Two-hander"),
           Speed = speed) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), k = sum(proc), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(`Proc rate` = sprintf("%.0f%%", k / n * 100),
         `95% interval` = sprintf("%.0f%% to %.0f%%", qbeta(0.025, k + 1, n - k + 1) * 100, qbeta(0.975, k + 1, n - k + 1) * 100)) %>%
  rename(`Landed white hits` = n, Procs = k) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Unbridled Wrath's proc rate for each weapon, by talent rank. Only hits below 100 rage are counted, since those are the ones where the rage gained tells us which weapon it was.")
```

```{r}
# Chance per hit = q x rank x speed^b. b = 0 is a fixed chance per hit, b = 1 is procs per minute.
ppm_fit <- glm(proc ~ log(speed) + offset(log(ubw_rank)), family = binomial(link = "log"),
               data = ubw_hand_rk, start = c(-2.6, 0))
ppm_b   <- coef(ppm_fit)[["log(speed)"]]
ppm_se  <- sqrt(vcov(ppm_fit)["log(speed)", "log(speed)"])
ppm_p   <- 2 * pnorm(-abs((ppm_b - 1) / ppm_se))
```

```{r fig.cap="Unbridled Wrath's proc rate per landed white hit against weapon speed, with each rank scaled to 5/5 (dots, with 95% intervals). A fixed chance per hit gives a flat line (solid); procs per minute would make it climb in line with weapon speed (dashed, pinned to the logs' average). The logs are flat.", fig.height=3.5}
ubw_speed <- ubw_hand_rk %>% group_by(speed) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), k = sum(proc), w = mean(5 / ubw_rank), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(rate = k / n * w, lo = qbeta(0.025, k + 1, n - k + 1) * w, hi = qbeta(0.975, k + 1, n - k + 1) * w)
flat <- sum(ubw_hand_rk$proc) / sum(ubw_hand_rk$ubw_rank / 5)
mean_speed <- weighted.mean(ubw_speed$speed, ubw_speed$n)
ggplot(ubw_speed, aes(speed, rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = flat, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_abline(slope = flat / mean_speed, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Weapon speed", y = "Procs per landed white hit (as 5/5)")
```

It isn't PPM. The proc chance per hit is the same whatever the weapon speed: at 5/5, Zomd's 1.8 off hand, 2.6 main hand and 3.8 two-hander all proc on roughly the same share of hits, when PPM would have the two-hander at about twice the off hand's rate. To put a number on it, we fitted one model across every rank and weapon where the chance per hit goes with weapon speed to some power: 0 means a fixed chance per hit, and 1 means PPM. The logs give **`r round(ppm_b, 2)`** (95% interval `r round(ppm_b - 1.96 * ppm_se, 2)` to `r round(ppm_b + 1.96 * ppm_se, 2)`), which is right on a fixed chance, and PPM is ruled out (`r if (startsWith(fmt_p(ppm_p), "<")) paste("p", fmt_p(ppm_p)) else paste("p =", fmt_p(ppm_p))`). This covers speeds from 1.8 to 3.8, and Nooch's 1.3 daggers (about 33% at 5/5, posted in the same issue) fit the same picture.

So once the fix lands, every weapon should get the same 60% chance per hit at 5/5, and faster weapons will get more procs per minute simply because they hit more often.

Two more things stay the same as before: every proc gives 1 rage with one-handers and 2 with two-handers, at every rank, and none of the procs come from Heroic Strike or Cleave. Blizzard's 1 Oct notes say the proc chance has been fixed ("a lower-than-intended proc chance"), and that two-handers now get 1 rage per proc like everyone else; neither has been checked in logs yet.

## Open questions

- Check the crit rule: does a white crit now give exactly twice a normal swing's rage? Do glancing blows still give the full rage?
- Check whether the rates change above level 17, the highest level in our logs. Logs from the live game can test this all the way to 60.
- Check that [BUG-1](#bug-ubw) is fixed. Blizzard's notes say it is, but no log since then has shown 5/5 procing on 60% of hits.
- Test Dual Wield Specialization. Its tooltip now says +50% off-hand rage at 5/5 (10% a rank), but Blizzard's notes say it lost its rage bonus. It's in the fourth row of the Fury tree, so it needs level 24 or higher.
- Test stances, and rage from damage taken, in a controlled setting. Since 2 November, higher level creatures have more health, which may change rage from damage taken.
- Test Reckless Swings. Does it give exactly 4 x 5 rage? Do Bloodthirst, Whirlwind, Heroic Strike and misses use up a charge? Is the extra rage doubled on a crit, or raised by Dual Wield Specialization on the off hand? The book assumes that landed attacks of any kind use a charge, and that the 5 rage is never multiplied.
- Check Flurry's 30% and Improved Whirlwind's 8-second cooldown in a log.
- Record mid-log hand swaps in the metadata, since one log shows both weapons being used in both hands.

## Changelog {#rage-changelog}

This chapter will keep changing as more logs come in, so each version of the findings gets a number in the form MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, plus the date it was published. The changelog only tracks the findings, so rewording or tidying up the text doesn't get a new version.

- **MAJOR** goes up when a conclusion changes, for example if a new log shows that rage does depend on damage after all, or that a rate is different from what we thought.
- **MINOR** goes up when we add findings without overturning what was there, like new logs that agree with the current results, or a new mechanic we've measured.
- **PATCH** goes up when we correct a number (a better estimate, or a fixed calculation) without changing any conclusion.

```{r}
changelog %>% rename(Version = version, Date = date, `What changed` = change) %>%
  knitr::kable(caption = "Versions of this chapter, newest first.")
```
